input: In this study, the rate constant of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was investigated at two temperatures in order to gain a better understanding of how the reaction rate responds to temperature. It is worth noting that the reaction is first order, which means that a single rate constant k, expressed in s-1, describes the rate at any given temperature. At 300 K, the rate constant k was measured as 0.071 s-1, whereas at 340 K, k was found to be 2.683 s-1, representing a substantial increase over the range studied. Importantly, the value at 340 K was not measured directly; instead, it was computed from the Arrhenius relation using an activation energy of 77 kJ mol-1, and it is therefore reported as a derived value. The activation energy of 77 kJ mol-1 plays a key role in this computation and underpins the derived figure. Each temperature was measured in triplicate in order to ensure reliability, and the relative standard deviation of k was 4%, highlighting the consistency and reproducibility of the measurements. Overall, between 300 K and 340 K, k rises from 0.071 s-1 to 2.683 s-1. It should also be noted that no rate constant is reported above 340 K, because above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, which made it impossible to collect samples without significant solvent loss. The relative standard deviation of 4% was obtained from the triplicate measurements spanning 300 K to the upper end of the range. In summary, the reported results comprise a measured rate constant at 300 K, a derived rate constant at 340 K, and a relative standard deviation of 4%, painting a comprehensive picture of the reaction kinetics across the accessible temperature range.
target: Rate constants for a first-order liquid-phase reaction were measured at two temperatures, 300 K and 340 K. The reaction is first order, so at a fixed temperature a single rate constant k, with units of s-1, sets the rate. At 300 K, k was 0.071 s-1. At 340 K, k was 2.683 s-1. The upper value was not measured directly; it was computed from the Arrhenius relation with an activation energy of 77 kJ mol-1, and it is reported here as a derived value. The activation energy of 77 kJ mol-1 enters the reported results only through that computation. Each temperature was measured in triplicate. The relative standard deviation of k was 4%. The triplicate measurements at the two temperatures carry that relative standard deviation of 4% in k. Between 300 K and 340 K, k rises from 0.071 s-1 to 2.683 s-1. The two temperatures are the only temperatures at which k is reported. No rate constant is reported above 340 K. Above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, and sampling loss set the upper end of the range. A value at any higher temperature would require sampling that the solvent loss prevents. The reported results are accordingly a measured rate constant at 300 K, a derived rate constant at 340 K, and a relative standard deviation of 4%, with no value above the upper temperature because the solvent evaporated during sampling.
